newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Analysts see signs of recovery in Taiwan surplus.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see signs of recovery in Taiwan surplus.

text.p: Economic analysts said on Thursday they divined signs of recovery in Taiwan's October trade surplus despite an eyebrow-raising downturn in exports by the island's prodigious electronics sector.
Taiwan had a trade surplus of US$532.4 million in October, down 62.2 percent from an October 1995 surplus of $1.41 billion, the biggest export month on record, the Finance Ministry said.

October exports fell a year-on-year 6.5 percent to $9.821 billion, while imports inched up 2.1 percent to $9.289 billion, the ministry said in a statement that indicated the recent export revival had run its course.
"This showed it's no longer boom time for exports," said David Yu, vice-president of International Investment Trust Co.
But experts said the export slowdown did not mean Taiwan's long-awaited recovery would be stillborn, citing important hints that the island's ailing "Asian dragon" economy was rebuilding.
Imports of capital goods, for example, rose a healthy five percent in October to $1.5 billion, while imports of consumer goods surged 48.5 percent, a clear sign of consumer confidence.

"Since June, capital goods imports have reversed the decline seen in the first half, indicating rising investment willingness that can help us to see an economic recovery," said Amy Huang, an economist at Nomura Securities.
Economist Yu said the consumer awakening boded well.
"This looks pretty good for an economic recovery because we have seen stagnant private consumption in the recent slowing economy," Yu said.
The ministry attributed October's reduced surplus to a decline in exports -- led by an 18.7 percent fall in exports from Taiwan's bedrock electronics sector.
The report played down the decrease, noting that October exports were the fourth highest on record but were being compared with the biggest month on the books.
Analysts said the slowing export growth was expected.
"We have forecast that the upward momentum for Taiwan's exports would slow down in the fourth quarter because the U.S. economy has reached its peak," Huang said.
The United States remained Taiwan's top export destination in October, taking 24.4 percent of the monthly total, despite a 1.5 percent year-on-year downturn to $2.394 billion.

Analysts also noted that Taiwan's record export pulse in October 1995 had been fuelled to a significant degree by a one-time marketing phenomenon -- U.S. software giant Microsoft Corp's launch of its Windows 95 software two months earlier.
The record-breaking launch stimulated strong sales for Taiwan-made computer systems.

Yu attributed the 18.7 percent electronics slide to a slowing growth in semiconductors, but said the telecommunication and information sector -- which includes computer systems -- still enjoyed a satisfying 15.2 percent export growth.
Analysts said the government still needed to do more to keep exports growing as Taiwan's sunset sectors -- textiles, plastics, electrical appliances and food -- fade in importance.
"The central bank may have to let the Taiwan dollar depreciate to boost exports, and we need improving relations between Taiwan and China to help boost the overall investment and economy," Yu said.
The ministry hailed Taiwan's success in transforming the labour-intensive industry into higher value-added high-tech and heavy industries.
The heavy and chemical industries, which include electronics and computers, accounted for 59.9 percent of cumulative January-October exports, up 2.1 percentage points year-on-year.
